name: Albedo Glacialis
specific_features: Surface reflectivity creates hazardous glare zone for approaching vessels
description: Albedo Glacialis is a world of blinding white, its ice surface polished by sublimation and wind into a mirror-smooth finish that reflects nearly all incident light back into space. The effect creates a paradox of illumination: the planet is one of the brightest objects in its system yet one of the coldest, as the high albedo prevents the surface from absorbing the stellar energy it so brilliantly reflects. Pressure ridge mountain ranges break the mirror plains where ice sheets collide, their jagged peaks the only rough texture on an otherwise glass-smooth world.

The thin atmosphere is transparent and pristine, offering no protection from the reflected glare that makes surface operations dangerous without polarized shielding. The light quality on the surface is extraordinary, every shadow crisp-edged and every detail illuminated by reflected skylight from the ice plains. The silence is enhanced by the smooth terrain, which provides no surfaces to generate or scatter sound.

Microbial life exists in the subsurface brine channels, where salt-concentrated liquid water persists in the spaces between ice crystals. These brine channels form a planet-spanning network of microscopic rivers, connecting microbial communities across thousands of kilometers. The organisms have adapted to extremely high salinity and near-freezing temperatures, metabolizing mineral salts dissolved from the rocky substrate beneath the ice.

Albedo Glacialis has attracted interest for solar energy applications, as the highly reflective surface could be used to concentrate stellar energy onto orbital collectors with minimal surface installation. The brine channel microbes have potential applications in extremophile biotechnology. The primary challenge for any operation is the surface glare, which has caused equipment malfunctions and crew disorientation in every expedition to date.
